newsitem.title: TAIWAN: GE won't accept Taiwan nuke plant delay - utility.
newsitem.headline: GE won't accept Taiwan nuke plant delay - utility.

text.p: U.S. contractor General Electric Corp has informed state-owned Taiwan Power Co that it will not extend a Wednesday midnight deadline for starting work on Taiwan's stalled fourth nuclear station, Taipower said.
"General Electric has given Taiwan Power a written notice stating its decision not to extend the deadline," utility vice president Lin Chin-chi told Reuters by telephone.
"This means that GE would be able to seek compensation (from Taipower) if parliament does not agree to support the project by midnight tonight," Lin said.

Despite GE's 1600 GMT Wednesday deadline, the fate of the US$4.1 billion power plant -- and GE's US$1.8 billion contract to supply its twin reactors and generators -- is not scheduled to be settled until a final parliamentary vote on Friday.
Parliament embarrassed Taipei in May by voting to cancel funding for the controversial project, but the government and Taipower have pushed ahead anyway, filing a formal appeal to parliament in June.
Parliament can make the cancellation stand only with a two-thirds vote of its members.

Debate was to have begun on Tuesday but opposition Democratic Progressive Party lawmakers effectively blocked any action by physically barring Premier Lien Chan from entering the building to explain the appeal and defend the project.
Taipower's Lin would not estimate how much GE might seek in compensation if the huge project is delayed beyond the contractual deadline, as this would be a matter for the courts.
"The issue would become a legal problem for Taiwan Power, so we can not estimate what a delay or cancel of the project would cost General Electric," Lin said.

GE officials declined to confirm or deny that they had made such a notice to Taipower or comment otherwise. GE has observed a strict "no comment" policy throughout the long showdown between Taiwan's parliament and the government.
Premier Lien, visibly angered by Tuesday's rebuff, said the opposition move represented a "dark day" for Taiwan's fledgling democracy and denounced the use of force rather than reason.
Lien had planned to deliver a report explaining Taiwan's energy policy and the island's need for the 2,700-megawatt fourth nuclear plant.
Analysts have been reluctant to say whether opponents could muster the votes necessary to make the cancellation stand.
Taipower, which has continued with work despite the deadlock and regards the nuclear project alive unless a final rejection is approved, asked GE in September to start work.
The utility, calling the plant necessary and safe, already has poured more than US$220 million into its construction.
Taiwan approved the plant in 1994 after years of delays and protests sparked by the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster in the Soviet Union.
A growing number of opponents in increasingly democratic Taiwan say nuclear power is dangerous and unnecessary if alternative energy sources are pursued.
